sectionToMerge.h2: Frequently Asked Questions About How Radiation Therapy Works: The Science Explained
sectionToMerge.intro: Radiation therapy is one of the most widely used cancer treatments, yet many patients want to understand the science behind it. These answers explain how radiation targets cancer cells, what to expect, and how eligibility, cost, and access are decided.

items.a: Radiation therapy works by delivering high-energy beams or particles that damage the DNA inside cancer cells, stopping them from growing and dividing. Because cancer cells often repair DNA damage less effectively than normal cells, they are more likely to die, while healthy tissue can recover. Treatment is carefully planned to target the tumour while limiting exposure to surrounding organs. The exact approach depends on cancer type, location, stage, and specialist review.

items.q: What is the science behind radiation killing cancer cells?
items.a: Radiation destroys cancer cells mainly by breaking the strands of DNA that carry a cell's genetic instructions. This damage is caused directly by the radiation or indirectly through charged particles called free radicals formed inside cells. When DNA damage becomes too severe to repair, the cell can no longer multiply and eventually dies. Rapidly dividing cancer cells are often more vulnerable to this effect, which is why radiation is used across many cancer types.

items.q: What types of radiation are used to treat cancer?
items.a: The main types of radiation used in cancer treatment are photon (X-ray) radiation, proton or particle radiation, and radioactive sources placed near a tumour. Photon-based external beam therapy is the most common, while proton therapy uses charged particles that may reduce dose to nearby tissue. Radioactive sources are used in brachytherapy and some systemic treatments. The choice depends on cancer type, tumour location, stage, and the treating team's assessment.

items.q: What is the difference between external beam radiation and brachytherapy?
items.a: External beam radiation delivers radiation from a machine outside the body, while brachytherapy places a radioactive source directly inside or next to the tumour. External beam therapy is aimed precisely at the cancer from different angles and is used for many tumour types. Brachytherapy allows a high dose to a small area with less exposure to distant tissue, and is common in prostate, cervical, and some other cancers. Selection depends on specialist review.

items.q: Who is eligible for radiation therapy?
items.a: Eligibility for radiation therapy depends on cancer type, stage, tumour location, previous treatments, and overall health. It may be considered as a main treatment, before or after surgery, alongside chemotherapy, or to relieve symptoms in advanced disease. Some patients may not be suitable if an area has already received high radiation doses or if certain health conditions raise risk. Final decisions should always be made by a qualified radiation oncology team after full assessment.

items.q: How is a radiation therapy plan created?
items.a: A radiation therapy plan is created using detailed imaging, usually a CT scan and sometimes MRI or PET scans, to map the exact location of the tumour. Specialists called radiation oncologists and medical physicists calculate the dose, angles, and number of sessions to target cancer while protecting healthy organs. This planning process, called simulation, may take several days. The plan is individualised and reviewed carefully before treatment begins.

Radiation therapy itself is painless during treatment, similar to having an X-ray, and most external beam sessions are quick and quiet. You do not feel the beam as it is delivered. However, side effects such as skin irritation, tiredness, or soreness in the treated area may develop over the course of treatment. These effects vary between patients and should be discussed with your care team, who can suggest ways to manage them.

items.q: What are the common side effects of radiation therapy?
items.a: Common side effects of radiation therapy include fatigue, skin changes in the treated area, and symptoms specific to the body region being treated. For example, chest radiation may cause a sore throat, while pelvic radiation may affect the bladder or bowel. Most side effects are temporary and improve after treatment ends, though some may appear later. The type and severity depend on the treatment site and dose, and should be monitored by your team.

items.q: How much does radiation therapy cost?
items.a: The cost of radiation therapy varies widely depending on the country, hospital, technique used, and number of sessions required. Advanced methods such as proton therapy or stereotactic radiosurgery generally cost more than standard external beam treatment. Final cost also depends on diagnosis, staging tests, treatment protocol, possible complications, and length of stay. Because pricing differs greatly between centres, patients should request a detailed estimate from the treating hospital before starting treatment.

items.q: Is radiation therapy available in India?
items.a: Radiation therapy is widely available in India, and many hospitals offer modern techniques such as IMRT, IGRT, stereotactic radiosurgery, and in some centres proton therapy. India is often chosen by international patients because advanced radiation technology may be available at a comparatively lower cost. Availability of a specific technique depends on the hospital and the patient's diagnosis. Suitability and final treatment planning should be confirmed by a qualified radiation oncology team.

items.q: Which countries offer advanced radiation therapy?
items.a: Advanced radiation therapy is offered in many countries, including India, the United States, Germany, the United Kingdom, Japan, China, and several others with specialised cancer centres. Techniques such as proton therapy and stereotactic radiosurgery are available only at selected hospitals because they require specific equipment and expertise. The best option for a patient depends on cancer type, technique needed, cost, and travel considerations, and should be guided by specialist advice.

items.q: What is proton beam therapy and how does it differ from X-ray radiation?
items.a: Proton beam therapy uses positively charged particles instead of X-rays to treat cancer, releasing most of their energy directly at the tumour and very little beyond it. This may reduce radiation dose to healthy tissue near the tumour, which can be helpful for tumours close to sensitive organs or in children. It is not necessarily better for every cancer, and availability is limited. Suitability should be assessed by a radiation oncology team.

items.q: What is stereotactic radiosurgery (SRS and SBRT)?
items.a: Stereotactic radiosurgery is a highly precise form of radiation that delivers very high doses to a small tumour in one or a few sessions, without surgery. When used in the brain it is called SRS, and when used elsewhere in the body it is often called SBRT. It requires accurate imaging and immobilisation to protect surrounding tissue. This approach may be suitable for selected small tumours, based on location, size, and specialist review.

Image-guided radiation therapy, or IGRT, uses scans taken just before or during each session to confirm the tumour's exact position before radiation is delivered. Because tumours and organs can shift slightly between sessions, this imaging helps the team target the cancer more accurately and protect nearby healthy tissue. IGRT is often combined with other advanced techniques. Whether it is appropriate depends on the tumour site and the treatment plan chosen by your specialists.

items.q: Are there clinical trials for radiation therapy?
items.a: Yes, clinical trials for radiation therapy study newer techniques, dose schedules, and combinations with drugs or immunotherapy. These trials aim to improve results or reduce side effects, but they cannot guarantee benefit to any individual patient. Eligibility is decided only after review of medical records and assessment by the trial investigators, and trials often have strict inclusion and exclusion criteria. Patients interested in trials should discuss suitable options with their treating oncology team.

items.q: What medical reports are needed to plan radiation therapy abroad?
items.a: To plan radiation therapy abroad, hospitals usually need recent imaging such as CT, MRI, or PET scans, pathology or biopsy reports, and a summary of previous treatments. Details of prior radiation are especially important to avoid over-exposing the same area. A current medical history and treating doctor's notes help specialists assess suitability and prepare an estimate. Access to treatment depends on hospital acceptance, medical review, and the patient's overall condition after evaluation.

items.q: How long does a course of radiation therapy take?
items.a: A course of radiation therapy can range from a single session to several weeks of daily treatments, depending on the technique and goal. Standard external beam therapy is often given five days a week for a few weeks, while stereotactic treatments may need only one to five sessions. Each daily session is usually short, lasting minutes. The exact schedule is individualised and confirmed by the radiation oncology team as part of treatment planning.

items.q: How does CancerFax help patients with radiation therapy?
items.a: CancerFax helps patients organise medical reports, identify relevant specialists or radiation treatment centres, estimate possible costs, and coordinate second opinions, appointments, travel, visa, and follow-up support. It does not provide treatment or replace doctors. Treatment decisions are always made by the qualified oncology team after reviewing the patient's diagnosis, stage, biomarkers, previous treatment, and overall health. Access to any centre depends on hospital acceptance, medical review, and the patient's condition.
